1600: They ordered me to hold the express, and somehow the express waited.
1601: They asked whether the train had a nicer carriage hidden somewhere, and were sad to learn it did not.
1602: They demanded the express not leave until they were comfortably seated, and it obeyed.
1603: They walked the platform slowly so everyone could watch, then held the train while they did it.
1604: They asked for the entire first carriage, and tipped me to keep it empty of anyone else.
1605: They told me to delay departure for their luggage, and the luggage was enormous.
1606: They wanted to know the train's top speed, then asked me to slow it down for a more dignified departure.
1607: They boarded last, on purpose, so the whole platform would wait and watch.
1608: They demanded the express be held, paid me generously for the trouble, and thanked no one else.
1609: They strolled to the platform as if the schedule was merely a suggestion for lesser travelers.
1610: They asked which train was the fastest, then insisted it wait a little longer for them.
1611: They handed me a fortune to keep the doors open one more grand minute.
1612: They ordered the conductor to announce their boarding, then waved at the announcement.
1613: They claimed the best window seat, drew the curtains, and had me guard the door.
1614: They made the whole train wait, tipped every porter, and boarded like a visiting monarch.
1615: They demanded the express hold, and when it did, they applauded the station for its good sense.
1616: They asked me to hold the train, and were so pleased with themselves I nearly held it forever.
1617: They boarded the express with more bags than the carriage wanted, and paid me to forget the count.
1618: They told me the schedule could wait, and against every rule I have, it did.
1619: They swept onto the platform, held up the express, and thanked the clock for its patience.
1620: They begged to go on air just to say hello to everyone, then talked for a glorious hour.
1621: They leaned into the microphone like an old friend and told the whole city how wonderful they were.
1622: They asked to say a quick hello, then thanked the microphone personally for listening.
1623: They wanted one minute on air and used it to introduce themselves eleven times.
1624: They read my whole script back to me, improved it, and signed off with their own name twice.
1625: They cradled the microphone as if it were the only thing that had ever understood them.
1626: They asked how many people were listening, heard the number, and decided it was almost enough for them.
1627: They asked for the microphone, said hello to the entire country, and refused to give it back.
1628: They insisted on live air, wished everyone a lovely day, and mostly wished it to themselves.
1629: They spoke into my microphone so tenderly I felt like I was intruding.
1630: They came in to say hello, and left having thanked their own reflection in the studio glass.
1631: They asked to greet the listeners, then asked the listeners to imagine how splendid they looked.
1632: They asked whether the microphone made them sound important, and refused to believe it was already off.
1633: They wanted just ten seconds on air, and spent the first nine describing how humble they were.
1634: They tapped the microphone, cleared their throat grandly, and told everyone they were hearing greatness.
1635: They borrowed the microphone for a moment and returned it warm and reluctant to let go.
1636: They read the weather, the news, and a long fond paragraph about themselves.
1637: They asked to say hello on air, and made it sound like the most important broadcast of the year.
1638: They went live to greet the audience, then thanked the audience for the privilege of hearing them.
1639: They held the microphone up like a trophy and dedicated their hello to their own good taste.
